analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 225-201 on May 25, 2006, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill repeals the federal ban on oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and orders the Interior Department to hold competitive lease sales on the refuge's coastal plain, starting with at least 200,000 acres within 22 months. It sets a minimum 12.5% royalty for the government, sends half the revenue to Alaska, and includes environmental limits like a 2,000-acre surface footprint cap and seasonal drilling restrictions. It also shortens environmental review, restricts public comment to 20 days, and sends all court challenges to one appeals court in Washington, D.C.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain access to a currently closed federal reserve believed to hold large oil deposits, with leases awarded by sealed competitive bids. Construction workers gain from a requirement that lessees negotiate project labor agreements, and Alaska Native corporations and workers get hiring preferences. Alaska's state government and North Slope communities gain revenue and capped impact aid.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to open the refuge's Coastal Plain to competitive oil and gas leasing, with a first sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months, and repeals the 1980 statutory ban on refuge drilling [S2] [S3].

Supporters argued it would create American jobs and domestic energy; the bill requires lessees to negotiate project labor agreements for construction work and to use best efforts to hire Alaska Natives and Native corporations, and bans export of oil produced under the leases [S4].

Sends 50% of leasing revenue to the State of Alaska and caps a $11 million impact-aid fund for North Slope communities like the City of Kaktovik and North Slope Borough to pay for police, water, medical, and other services strained by drilling [S3] [S4].

Imposes environmental conditions including a 2,000-acre cap on surface development, a 'no significant adverse effect' standard, seasonal drilling limits, and up to 45,000 acres of protected Special Areas where no surface occupancy is allowed [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: The public gives up undisturbed wilderness and wildlife habitat in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, permanently if development proceeds. Federal taxpayers get a guaranteed royalty of only 12.5% of production value, half of which goes to Alaska. Citizens challenging drilling face shortened environmental review, a 20-day comment window, and a requirement to take all cases to a single federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., where the government's analysis is presumed correct.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and the refuge itself

drawbacks.text: The bill deems a 1987 environmental impact statement sufficient for pre-lease decisions and orders the Secretary to analyze only a leasing and a single alternative — no non-leasing option — while limiting public comments to a 20-day window [S3] [S4].

All legal challenges must be filed within 90 days in the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, where the Secretary's environmental analysis is presumed correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence, making it much harder for citizens or conservation groups to stop or slow drilling in court [S4].

The bill locks in a minimum royalty of only 12.5% on a public resource and strips the Interior Secretary of any authority to close refuge lands to drilling beyond what the bill itself allows [S3] [S4].

Even with the 2,000-acre footprint cap and Special Areas, drilling in the refuge's Coastal Plain would introduce industrial development into one of the country's most intact wilderness areas, with permanent effects on caribou, birds, and subsistence hunting communities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs real but modest public benefits — some jobs, Alaska revenue sharing, and genuine environmental stipulations — against a one-way, permanent opening of a national wildlife refuge to industry, with expedited court review and narrow environmental analysis making it hard to revisit. The guaranteed 12.5% royalty is at the low end of federal terms, so the public shares less in the resource's value than it would under many other leases. The design favors getting leases issued quickly over careful review.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in May 2006, but the Senate let it sit on its calendar without a vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Pombo introduced the bill on May 19, 2006, and it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee [S1] [S6].
The House took it up under a rule that closed the bill to amendments, and passed it 225-201 on May 25, 2006, with 198 of 231 Republicans voting yes and only 27 of 201 Democrats [S6] [S8].

Before passage, Rep. George Miller offered a motion to recommit — a last-chance amendment — that would have disqualified companies holding older Interior Department leases with unlimited royalty relief from bidding; it failed 201-223 [S6] [S7].
The Senate received the bill, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar on June 5, 2006, but never brought it to a vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S6] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a Senate vote, the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge remained closed to drilling, and the conservation groups and members who opposed opening it were better off. Oil companies did not gain the access the bill would have provided.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party: 198 of 231 Republicans voted yes while only 27 of 201 Democrats did; on the Miller motion to recommit, 177 of 201 Democrats voted yes versus 23 of 230 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would open a closed federal wildlife refuge to competitive oil and gas leasing at a minimum 12.5% royalty, with narrow environmental review and court challenges funneled to a single friendly venue. The industry's gain comes from extracting a public resource on protected public land on fixed terms that the public could not tighten later.

The bill requires lessees to negotiate project labor agreements for production and construction work and to use best efforts to hire Alaska Natives, creating union-scale jobs tied to development. These benefits depend on drilling actually proceeding.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations and North Slope communities
industries.note: Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation would receive long-pending land conveyances, and communities would get an $11 million-capped impact aid fund plus hiring preferences. The same communities face pressure on subsistence hunting and local services from the development the bill invites.

The bill repeals the statutory drilling ban in the refuge and strips the Interior Secretary of independent authority to close Coastal Plain lands, locking development in. Their interest runs with keeping an intact public wilderness and subsistence hunting grounds undisturbed.
